# Hemavata Sutta (Snp 1.9 (PTS Snp 27))

**ID:** Snp 1.9 (PTS Snp 27)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Hemavata Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Hemavata Sutta* (Snp 1.9) is the ninth discourse of the *Uragavagga* in the *Suttanipāta* [Norman 1983; Anderson and Smith 1913]. In the collection's *uddāna* and commentary (*Paramatthajotikā* II), it is also designated by the alternative title *Sātāgira Sutta* [Norman 1997-2001; Anderson and Smith 1913]. The text is structured as a living dialogue opening on the fifteenth *uposatha* night between two spirit deities (*yakkhas*), Sātāgira and Hemavata, who discuss the virtues and spiritual attainments of the Buddha [Katre 1931; Norman 1983; DeCaroli 1999; Anderson and Smith 1913]. After this preliminary exchange (verses 1–15), they approach the Buddha personally and present a series of inquiries [Katre 1931; Norman 1983; DeCaroli 1999]. In response, the Buddha explains how one escapes suffering, how one crosses over the flood, and what manner of clinging (*upādāna*) harasses the world [Bodhi 2003]. The sutta concludes with stanzas in praise of the Buddha and the conversion of the two interlocutors and their retinue of one thousand spirits [Katre 1931; DeCaroli 1999].

 DharmaNexus corroborates these cross-language alignments with numerous matches in both Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* recensions (T 99 and T 100), while also finding alignments with the Patna Dharmapada and Tibetan texts such as the *Yogācārabhūmi* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records text reuse between Snp 1.9 (§18.1–19.5) and the *Devatā Saṁyutta* (SN 1), matching parallel inquiries on escaping suffering [DharmaNexus; Bodhi 2003]. Canonical and post-canonical texts cite or reuse the sutta, including the *Nettippakaraṇa*, the *Kathāvatthu*, later cosmological treatises like the *Lokapaññatti*, and Chinese texts such as T 1644 [Norman 1983; Vallée Poussin and Pruden 1988].
